Surah 61: Al-Saff

Medinan, though it is said to be Meccan. Its verses number fourteen.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The discussion of it is like that which passed concerning its counterpart.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 2:

﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ It is related that the Muslims said: "If we knew the most beloved of deeds to Allah, the Exalted, we would spend our wealth and our selves on it." Then when jihad was prescribed, they disliked it, and so this was revealed. As for what is said, that the verse revealed was His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row﴾, it is clearly invalid. It is also related that "they said: O Messenger of Allah, if we knew the most beloved of deeds to Allah, the Exalted, we would hasten to it. So it was revealed: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce?﴾ up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your selves﴾," and then they turned away on the day of Uhud. In this there is an implication that the order of the noble verses is not according to the order of their revelation. It is also said: when Allah, the Exalted, informed of the reward of the martyrs of Badr, the Companions said: "O Allah, bear witness: if we meet battle, we will exert our utmost effort in it," but then they fled on the day of Uhud, and so this was revealed. It is also said: it was revealed concerning one who praises himself falsely, when a man would say: "I killed," when he had not killed, and "I struck," when he had not struck, and so on. It is also said: a man had harmed the Muslims on the day of Badr and inflicted damage upon them, then Suhayb killed him, and another claimed his killing, so this was revealed concerning the one who claimed it. It is also said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and their calling with faith is mockery, and their faith is not so, as you will come to know. And "li-ma" is composed of the preposition "li" (for) and the interrogative "ma" (what), whose alif has been dropped for lightness, due to their frequent use together, as in ʿamma and fima and their like, meaning: "for what reason do you say that you will do the good and the right which you do not do?" Yet the real purpose of the rebuke and reproach is their not doing it, and they were addressed concerning their saying in order to draw attention to the multiplication of their disobedience, by clarifying that the reprehensible thing is not only abandoning the promised good, but also the promise of it, while they had been thinking it to be good. Had it been said, "Why do you not do what you say?", it would have been understood from it that the reprehensible thing is the abandoning of the promise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 3:

﴿Greatly hateful it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.﴾ This is an explanation of the extreme ugliness of what they did and the excessive repugnance of it. "Kabura" (how great it is) is from the pattern of "ni'ma" and "bi'sa" (the verbs of praise and blame), in which there is an ambiguous pronoun (damir mubham) explained by the indefinite noun that follows it, and "an taqulu" ("that you say") is the thing praised or blamed (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm). It has been said: in it is intended the expression of amazement (ta'ajjub) without its wording, and it is attributed to "an taqulu"; and the accusative of "maqtan" (hatred) as a specification (tafsir) of it indicates that their saying what they do not do is pure hatred, unmixed with anything, which is great in the sight of one before whom every great thing is considered insignificant.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as though they were a solid structure﴾ is an explanation of what is pleasing to Him, the Exalted, after the explanation of what is abhorrent to Him. This is explicit that what they said refers to the promise of fighting, not to what the boaster declared, what the pretender claimed, or what the hypocrite repeated; and that the focus of the reproach and rebuke is their failure to fulfill it, not their promise itself, as has been indicated. It has been read as "yuqātalūna" (with a fatha on the ta', "they are fought") and as "yuqātilūna" (they fight). "Ṣaffan" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that takes the place of the active or passive participle, and its accusative case is adverbial of state (ḥāl) from the subject of "yuqātilūna," meaning: lining themselves up in rows, or arranged in rows. The Almighty's saying: ﴿as though they were a solid structure﴾ is a state (ḥāl) from the hidden pronoun in the first state, meaning: likened, in their close-packed alignment without gap or fissure, to a structure whose parts are fixed to one another and piled together until they become one single thing.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 61, verse 5:

Allah's saying, ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾, is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) that confirms what preceded it regarding the abomination of abandoning fighting. The word ﴿إذْ﴾ (idh, "when") is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul bihi) governed by an implied verb, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) through a shift of address (talwin). The meaning is: "Mention to these people who turned away from fighting the time when Moses said to the Children of Israel, when he urged them to fight the tyrants, with his saying: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will turn back as losers﴾. But they did not comply with his command and disobeyed him most severely, when they said: ﴿O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants, and we will never enter it until they leave it. But if they leave it, then we will enter﴾, up to His saying: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾. They persisted in that and harmed him, peace be upon him, with every kind of harm."

﴿O my people, why do you harm me﴾: that is, by opposing and disobeying me in what I have commanded you. His saying, ﴿while you know that I am the messenger of Allah to you﴾, is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) that emphasizes the denial of harm and the negation of its cause. The particle ﴿قَدْ﴾ (qad) serves to affirm knowledge, and the present-tense form indicates its continuity. The meaning is: "And the situation is that you know, with certain and continuous knowledge, by witnessing the overpowering miracles that appeared at my hands, most of which was the destruction of your enemy and your deliverance from his dominion, that I am the messenger of Allah to you, to guide you to the good of this world and the Hereafter. And part of the requirement of your knowledge of this is that you should exalt me greatly and hasten to obey me."

﴿So when they deviated﴾: that is, they persisted in deviating from the truth which Moses, peace be upon him, had brought, and they continued in it.

﴿Allah turned their hearts away﴾: that is, He diverted them from accepting the truth and inclining toward what is right, because their choice was turned toward error and misguidance. His saying, ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, is an concluding parenthetical clause (iʿtiraḍ tadhyili) that confirms the content of what precedes regarding the turning away and indicates its cause. The meaning is: He does not guide, with a guidance that leads to what guidance leads to, the people who go outside obedience and the path of truth and persist in deviation. Its scope is general to all. The intended people are either: those mentioned specifically, and the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves to condemn them with defiance and to make defiance the cause of the lack of guidance; or the category of defiant people, who are included in the ruling primarily. Whichever it is, describing them with defiance refers to what is in His saying: ﴿So separate us from the defiant people﴾. This is what the eloquence of the noble composition requires and what sound taste approves. As for what has been said in the context of explaining the causes of the harm, namely that they harmed him, peace be upon him, with various kinds of harm, such as belittling and disparaging him personally, denying his signs, disobeying him in matters that would benefit them, worshipping the calf, their request to see Allah openly, and denial, which is the neglect of Allah's right and his own right, these have no connection to this context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when Jesus, the son of Mary, said﴾ is either conjoined to the first "when" (idh) and governed by its governing element, or it is governed by a concealed verb conjoined to its governing element.

﴿O Children of Israel﴾: he addressed them thus to win over their hearts toward believing him in his saying ﴿Indeed, I am the messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾, for his confirmation of it, upon him be prayer and peace, is among the strongest incentives for them to believe him. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and bringing good tidings of a messenger who will come after me﴾ is conjoined to "confirming" (muşaddiqan), serving as an incentive to believe him, upon him be prayer and peace, in the same way, insofar as the good tidings of him occur in the Torah. The governing element for both is what is contained in "messenger" of the meaning of sending, not the prepositional phrase, for that is a complement (ṣilah) of "messenger," and complements are far from including the meaning of a verb, and the function of governance revolves around this. That is: "I have been sent to you while confirming what preceded me of the Torah and bringing good tidings of a messenger who will come after me."

﴿his name is Ahmad﴾: that is, Muhammad ﷺ. He means that my religion is the confirmation of the books of God and His prophets, all of them, of those who came before and after. It is also read "min ba'di" with the yā' vowelled with a fatḥah.

﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs﴾: that is, with the manifest miracles.

﴿they said, "This is clear sorcery."﴾ Pointing to what he brought, or to him, upon him be prayer and peace. Calling it sorcery is for emphasis (mubālaghah), and it is supported by the reading of one who recited "this is a sorcerer" (hadha sahir).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 7:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam?﴾ That is: which of the people is more unjust than one who is invited to Islam, the religion that brings him to the happiness of both abodes, yet he places in the position of response the fabrication against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by his saying of His speech, which is the calling of His servants to the truth, "This is plain magic." That is: he is more unjust than every wrongdoer, even though the apparent wording of the speech does not explicitly negate equality, and its explanation has passed more than once. It has also been read as "yuddaʿā" (يُدَّعى). It is said: "daʿāhu" and "idda'āhu," like "lamasahu" and "iltamasahu."

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ That is: He does not guide them to what contains their success, because they do not turn toward it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 61, verse 8:**

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾. That is: they wish to extinguish His religion, or His Book, or His clear proof. The *lam* here is *zā'idah* (superfluous, an added particle with no independent meaning), because the verb carries the sense of wishing (*irādah*), and it is added to reinforce it, just as it is added to reinforce the sense of possession (*idāfah*) in the expression *lā abā laka* ("may you have no father"). Or it means: they wish to extinguish the light of Allah by slander.

﴿with their mouths﴾: by their attacks against it. Their condition is likened to that of one who blows on the light of the sun with his mouth in order to extinguish it.

﴿But Allah will perfect His light﴾: that is, He will bring it to its goal by spreading it throughout the horizons and making it prevail. It was also read as *mutimmun nūrah* (with the noun *nūrah* in the accusative and without the possessive suffix on the participle), without *idāfah* (the genitive construction).

﴿even though the disbelievers dislike it﴾: as a humiliation (*irghām*) for them. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hāl*), as has been explained repeatedly. (p-245)

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 9:**

﴿He it is Who sent His Messenger with the guidance﴾, that is, with the Qur'an or with the miracle.

﴿and the religion of truth﴾, and the upright creed (al-millah al-hanifiyyah).

﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, that is, that He may make it exalted over all the religions that oppose it. Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic and Exalted, has fulfilled His promise, for He has made it such that no religion among the religions remains except that it is overcome and subdued by the religion of Islam.

﴿Though the polytheists dislike it﴾ that, and it has been recited as "He it is Who sent His Prophet" (nabiyyahu).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 10:**

﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ It is also read "تُنَجِّيكُمْ" (tunajjikum) with the doubled letter (shaddah) on the jim, meaning "will deliver you" with intensification.

The Most High's words: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ are a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that comes as an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as if they had said: "How should we act, or what should we do?" So it was said: "You believe in Allah..." etc. It is a declarative statement that carries the meaning of a command, brought to signal the obligation of compliance, so it is as though the act has already occurred, and so it reports its occurrence. This is supported by the reading of those who read "Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive" (āminū, jāhidū, in the imperative), and it is also read as "tu'minū" and "tujāhidū" with the imperative lām (lām al-amr) being implied.

﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of faith and struggle in its two forms, and the sense of distance in it is due to what has passed more than once.

﴿is better for you﴾ absolutely, or better than your wealth and your lives.

﴿if you know﴾ meaning: if you are among the people of knowledge, for the ignorant are not regarded for their actions; or, if you know that it is better for you, it will be better for you then, because when you know that and believe it, you will love faith and struggle more than you love your own selves and your wealth, and so you will be sincere and you will prosper.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 12:

﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾ is the answer (jawab) to a command implied by the wording of a statement, or to a condition, or to a question which the speech indicates. Its estimated sense is: "If you believe and strive (in jihad)," or "Would you accept that I guide you to something that will forgive you?" Taking it as the answer to "Shall I guide you?" is far-fetched, because mere guidance does not necessitate forgiveness.

﴿And He will admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence (adn). That is﴾ i.e., what has been mentioned of forgiveness and admission into the gardens, described with the sublime qualities that have been mentioned.

﴿the great triumph﴾ beyond which there is no triumph.

﴿And another﴾ blessing, besides these great blessings, is for you: a swift one.

﴿that you love﴾: that you desire and long for. It contains an allusion (*ta'rid*) that they prefer the swift to the lasting. It has also been said that *"ukhrā"* (أُخْرى) is in the accusative by implying "yu'tikum" (يُعْطِكُمْ, "He will give you") or "tuḥibbūna" (تُحِبُّونَ, "you love"), or that it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿help from Allah﴾. On the first reading, ﴿help from Allah﴾ is a substitution (*badal*) or an explanatory apposition (*bayān*). On the reading that puts it in the accusative, it is the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿and a near victory﴾, meaning a swift one, is conjoined (*'aṭf*) to "naṣr" (نَصْرٌ, "help") according to the aforementioned possibilities. It was also recited as *"naṣran"* (نَصْرًا) and *"fatḥan qarīban"* (فَتْحًا قَرِيبًا), in the accusative either by specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*) or as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: you will be helped with help, and a victory will be opened for you as a victory. Or they are in apposition (*badaliyya*) to "ukhrā" (أُخْرى) on the assumption that it is in the accusative, meaning: He will give you another blessing, help and victory.

﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is conjoined to an omitted phrase like "qul yā ayyuhā alladhīna" (قُلْ يَأيُّها الَّذِينَ, "say, O you who") and "wa-bashshir" (وبَشِّرْ, "and give good tidings"). Or it is conjoined to "tu'minūna" (تُؤْمِنُونَ, "you believe"), since it has the meaning of "āminū" (آمِنُوا, "believe"), as if it were said: believe and strive, O believers, and give them good tidings, O Messenger, of what I have promised them for that, in the swift and the lasting.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 61, verse 14:

﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾. It was also read as "anṣāran lillāh" (helpers for Allah) without the construct, because the meaning is "be some of the helpers of Allah." It was also read as "kūnū antum anṣāra Allāh" (you yourselves be the helpers of Allah).

﴿As Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who will be my helpers for Allah?"﴾ That is: who will be my soldiers, heading toward Allah, as His saying the Exalted requires: ﴿The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah"﴾. The first idafah (construct) is the annexation of one of two partners to the other, because of the particular relationship between them. The second is the annexation of the agent to the object, and the comparison is in respect of meaning. That is: be helpers of Allah just as the disciples were His helpers when Jesus said to them: ﴿Who will be my helpers for Allah?﴾ Or say to them: be as Jesus said to the disciples. The disciples (al-ḥawāriyyūn) were his chosen companions (aṣfiyā'uhu), and they were the first to believe in him, and they were twelve men.

﴿So a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾. That is: in Jesus, and they obeyed him in what he commanded them of supporting the religion.

﴿And another group disbelieved﴾ in him, and they fought them.

﴿So We supported those who believed against their enemy﴾. That is: We strengthened them with proof or with the sword, and that was after Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised up.

﴿So they became dominant﴾, victorious.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Saff, Jesus will send blessings upon him and seek forgiveness for him as long as he is in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be his companion."
